title: Same-Origin Policy & CORS Pitfalls
objectives: Explain what the Same-Origin Policy protects and what it does not
Configure CORS correctly for public and credentialed requests
Recognize why wildcard origins plus credentials is a dangerous misconfiguration
Contrast what CORS governs with what CSRF exploits
body:
The Same-Origin Policy (SOP) is the browser's core isolation rule: script from origin A may read responses from origin B only if the server explicitly allows it via CORS. SOP is a defense you get for free; CORS (Cross-Origin Resource Sharing) is the narrow, deliberate door you cut through it. Most CORS bugs are doors cut far wider than intended.

## The problem
Your API needs to serve your SPA at `app.example.com`, so someone configures `Access-Control-Allow-Origin: *`. Then the API also authenticates users with cookies, and the team wants to know why the security review failed — and what the dangerous version of this configuration would look like.

## Constraints
- CORS only governs whether a cross-origin script can *read* a response; browsers still *send* cross-origin requests freely (that is CSRF territory).
- With credentials (cookies, HTTP auth), the spec forbids `Access-Control-Allow-Origin: *`; the server must echo one exact origin.
- `Access-Control-Allow-Credentials: true` is what turns an echoed origin into a credentialed read.
- Reflecting *any* incoming Origin header back, together with credentials, means every website can read your API as the visiting user.
- Preflights (OPTIONS) only gate certain requests; simple GET/POST still fire without one.

## Options
```json
{
  "dangerous": {
    "Access-Control-Allow-Origin": "*",
    "Access-Control-Allow-Credentials": "true",
    "why": "spec-forbidden combo; some frameworks silently reflect origin instead, which is the real-world version of this bug"
  },
  "dangerousReflection": {
    "notes": "origin echoed from request without allowlist",
    "effect": "evil.example.com reads responses with the user's cookies attached",
    "defense": "compare Origin against a server-side allowlist; never reflect blindly"
  },
  "correctCredentialed": {
    "Access-Control-Allow-Origin": "https://app.example.com",
    "Access-Control-Allow-Credentials": "true",
    "Vary": "Origin",
    "why": "exact trusted origin, credentials on, cache keyed by origin"
  },
  "correctPublic": {
    "Access-Control-Allow-Origin": "*",
    "why": "public data, no cookies — wildcard is fine here"
  }
}
```

## Tradeoffs
Strict allowlists mean every new frontend subdomain needs a config change — friction, but the honest price of safety. `Vary: Origin` is required once responses differ per origin, or a shared cache can hand one origin's headers to another. Skipping CORS headers entirely is also a valid choice: cross-origin readers get nothing, and same-origin pages are unaffected.

## Decision
Default to no CORS. For public, credential-free data, use the wildcard. For anything session-backed, echo an exact origin from a server-side allowlist with `Access-Control-Allow-Credentials: true` and `Vary: Origin`. Never reflect arbitrary origins, and keep state-changing endpoints protected against CSRF regardless of CORS (next lesson).

## Measure it
Verification is concrete: from a not-your-origin page, attempt a credentialed fetch to each API class and assert it fails to read; from your SPA, assert it succeeds. Add an integration test that sends `Origin: https://evil.example` with cookies and expects the response to be unreadable (no ACAO header). Re-run after every CORS change.

## Best practices
- Keep a server-side origin allowlist; never reflect the Origin header unvalidated.
- Use credentials only on endpoints that need them, with exact-origin ACAO.
- Add `Vary: Origin` when responses vary per origin to protect shared caches.
- Test CORS from a real third-party origin, not just the happy path.
- Treat CORS and CSRF as separate problems with separate defenses.

## Common mistakes
- Enabling `ACAO: *` plus credentials in dev and letting the config leak to production.
- Echoing any Origin to make an integration go away, handing every site a credentialed read.
- Assuming CORS blocks request *sending* — it only blocks response reading.
- Caching responses without `Vary: Origin`, leaking one origin's CORS headers to another.
- Debugging CORS by disabling browser security instead of fixing headers.

## Production considerations
- Store the origin allowlist in config per environment; staging origins must not appear in production lists.
- Alert on responses that carry both wildcard ACAO and `Allow-Credentials` — a config drift detector in CI catches this in seconds.
- Review CORS config when adding a new first-party domain or embedded widget.
- Remember internal APIs are reachable by any browser too; SOP/CORS hygiene applies behind the VPN as well.

examples.name: cors-check.js

exercise.prompt: Build a CORS config auditor. Each config lists its ACAO value and whether Allow-Credentials is set. Render a verdict per config: blocked-by-spec when ACAO is * with credentials; dangerous when ACAO reflects unknown origins with credentials; ok-credentialed for an exact allowlisted origin with credentials; ok-public for * without credentials. Implement the auditor.
hints: Wildcard + credentials is the first check — it is forbidden by the spec outright.
reflect-any with credentials lets any site read as the user: dangerous, not ok.
Only exact allowlisted origins with credentials are ok-credentialed.

questions.prompt: Why is Access-Control-Allow-Origin: * combined with Access-Control-Allow-Credentials: true dangerous (and forbidden)?
options: It disables TLS on the connection
Any website could read API responses with the victim's cookies attached
It makes the browser send two requests
It only fails on HTTP/3 connections
questions.explanation: Credentialed requests carry the user's session; a wildcard read permission would let any origin read authenticated data as that user, which is why the spec forbids the combination.

options: Whether a cross-origin request may be sent at all
Whether a cross-origin script may read the response
Whether the server accepts POST requests
questions.explanation: Browsers send cross-origin requests regardless; CORS decides if the initiating script gets to read the response. Request sending is the CSRF problem instead.
